speaker: Alex Schultz
title: Meta CMO: How Advertising Works Under the Hood
question: In consumer retail, how do modern retail media networks actually work under the hood compared to traditional brand advertising?
guest: One thing that goes on deeper in the retail ad network funnel—beyond Walmart and Amazon—is smaller retailers also buy off other companies with their first-party data so the retail ad network becomes a third-party ad network as well, which creates space for things to go really badly in terms of fraud, attribution, and ads showing up in the wrong place. From the perspective of an FMCG company or quick-serve restaurant—where DoorDash and Uber Eats are retail ad networks too—they're getting a double bite of the cherry from the people retailing their goods: they have to pay for placement to promote themselves, and they have to pay a commission to the vendor. But it's also just history. You paid for placement on the shelves in Walmart, and you paid for placement in the Sears catalog. Retail ad networks have existed as long as retailers have existed; all this has done is modernize that and bring it online. It's going more to below-the-line media budgets—direct response, placement-related, discount-related budgets—and less to above-the-line media buying. And it all boils down to data, algorithms, and first-party data having an advantage over third-party data.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Retail media networks turn a retailer's own shopper data and properties into an ad business. Traditional brand advertising buys reach against broad audiences (TV, print, open-web display) using demographic proxies or third-party data, and it measures success indirectly through surveys, reach metrics or statistical models, because the ad exposure and the sale happen in different systems.

A retail media network collapses that gap. The retailer holds first-party data tied to logged-in or loyalty identities: searches, browsing, baskets and purchases. Advertisers bid in auctions, usually cost-per-click, for sponsored product listings in search results and category pages, where ranking blends bid with relevance and predicted conversion. The same audience data is also used to target display, video and connected-TV ads off-site through demand-side platforms, and increasingly in-store screens.

Because the retailer also owns the transaction, it can match ad exposure to actual SKU-level sales, online and in-store, which is called closed-loop attribution. Data clean rooms let brands analyse this without receiving raw customer data.

The caveats are that retailers grade their own results, standards vary across networks, and much of the spend is reallocated trade-promotion money capturing existing demand rather than creating new demand.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Traditional brand advertising buys broad demographic proxies or third-party segments across disconnected media channels, relying on probabilistic models or panel surveys to infer whether an impression eventually drove a sale. Modern retail media networks replace that guesswork with a deterministic ad-tech stack built directly atop a retailer’s first-party identity graph of loyalty accounts, browsing behavior, and historical point-of-sale transactions.

Under the hood, brands bid via self-serve platforms in real-time auctions where the retailer’s ad server scores bid prices alongside predicted conversion probability, search relevance, and live SKU inventory—automatically pausing spend when local shelves run dry. Onsite, sponsored products render natively inside search and category pages at the exact moment of purchase intent. Offsite, retailers match hashed shopper IDs with connected TV, social, and open-web publishers inside privacy-safe data clean rooms, targeting verified category buyers without exposing raw customer data. Crucially, because the same identity spine links ad impressions to both online checkouts and physical register scans, retail media delivers closed-loop attribution, tying ad spend directly to verified, SKU-level transactions and incremental sales lift.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Retail media networks (Amazon Ads, Walmart Connect, Roundel at Target, Kroger Precision Marketing) turn a retailer's first-party shopper data and digital real estate into an ad business. Under the hood, the retailer ties logged-in identities, loyalty cards and payment data to every purchase, online and in store. Brands then bid in real-time auctions, usually cost-per-click, for sponsored product slots in search results, on product pages and in apps. They can also buy offsite display and CTV audiences built from purchase data, either through the retailer's own DSP or through data clean rooms, as well as in-store screens. The key piece is closed-loop measurement. Because the retailer owns both the ad exposure and the cash register, it can report return on ad spend tied to actual SKU-level sales, sometimes including incremental lift.

Traditional brand advertising, like TV, print and programmatic display, buys broad reach based on demographics or context. It's priced by CPM and measured indirectly through brand-lift surveys, panels or media-mix modeling, with no direct link to purchases. Retail media budgets often come out of trade marketing money, and margins are high because the retailer already owns the inventory and data. That's why these networks have become major profit centers.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Modern retail media networks (RMNs) like Amazon Ads or Walmart Connect operate on a closed-loop ad tech stack powered by first-party transaction data, whereas traditional brand advertising relies on broad reach, third-party proxies, and estimated lift. Under the hood, an RMN links a retailer’s ad server and auction engine directly to loyalty accounts, browsing logs, and point-of-sale systems. When a shopper searches or browses, a real-time auction ranks sponsored products and display ads by combining bid price with predicted purchase relevance. Retailers can also extend these audiences off-site to connected TV or the open web through privacy-safe data clean rooms. After an impression or click, the network deterministically matches ad exposure against actual online and in-store SKU-level receipts. Unlike traditional TV or print campaigns that depend on delayed panel surveys or econometric modeling, RMNs deliver rapid attribution tied directly to verifiable sales and return on ad spend.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Retail media networks turn a retailer’s ad space and shopping data into an advertising business. A brand can bid to place a sponsored product in search results, buy a display ad on the retailer’s site, or pay to reach the retailer’s shoppers on other websites or streaming TV. The network can use search terms to decide which ad to show or build audiences from browsing and purchase history. When it can match an ad impression or click to a shopper’s account or loyalty ID, it can link that exposure to a later purchase online or in-store.

Traditional brand advertising typically buys reach and frequency through TV, print, or other media, then estimates sales impact through surveys, sales trends, or experiments. Retail media’s distinctive advantage is that the retailer already sees what people buy, so it can report which sales followed an ad. That attribution alone can’t tell the brand how many sales the ad caused. A randomized holdout can estimate that lift.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A retail media network lets brands buy ads using a retailer’s shopper data and measure whether those ads lead to purchases. If you search a grocery app for coffee, a brand can bid for a sponsored spot. The retailer weighs the bid and the ad’s relevance to decide what appears. Brands can also reach audiences such as past coffee buyers on streaming TV or other sites through the retailer’s ad partners.

The main difference from traditional brand advertising is the link to the checkout. A conventional TV campaign buys access to a program’s audience and typically measures reach, brand awareness, or changes in overall sales. A retailer can often use account or loyalty data to match an ad impression or click to a later online or in-store purchase and report the resulting sales to the brand in aggregate. That match shows a shopper saw the ad and then bought the product. Estimating how many extra sales the ad caused requires a comparison, such as a randomly selected group that didn’t see it.
